newsitem.title: FRANCE: China dissident's sister says West backs tyrants.
newsitem.headline: China dissident's sister says West backs tyrants.

text.p: The sister of Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng, winner of the 1996 Sakharov prize, lashed out on Wednesday at Western backing for the Chinese government.
"No one in the West can ignore the fact that supporting the Communist regime is akin to supporting a gang of tyrants," Shanshan Wei-Blank told reporters at the European Parliament.
She was speaking at a news conference after receiving the "Sakharov prize for freedom of thought" on behalf of her brother from the parliament's president, Klaus Haensch.
Wei, now 49, has spent most of the last two decades in prison in China for his outspoken comments on human rights and political issues. Last December he was given a 14-year sentence.

"The Chinese government brutally represses minorities. Yet throughout the world, statesmen allow themselves to be deluded by the mirage of the great Chinese 'market of the future', focusing narrowly on trade with China," Wei-Blank said.
The Chinese mission to the European Union has harshly criticised the EU's directly elected assembly for awarding the 15,000 Ecu ($18,740) prize to someone who it said was "a common criminal".

"This encourages and supports activities against the Chinese government, it is also a brutal interference in the internal affairs and sovereign jurisdiction of China," the mission said in a letter to Haensch in October.
Wei-Blank said that those who tolerated the actions of Beijing were hindering peaceful change inside China.

"Everyone should realise that tolerating the Communist Party's crazed oppression of the peaceful and reasonable efforts of Chinese democrats means that China will miss the chance of harmonious change," she told reporters.

She said at the award ceremony that by giving the Sakharov prize to Wei, the parliament was greatly encouraging the democracy movement inside China at a time when it faced "repression from the Chinese government and a lack of response on the part of all the major countries in the world."

"For the sake of the people of China, we want an open and free dialogue with the Chinese leadership, not only on trade and investment but also on respect for human rights," Haensch told the ceremony, held at the assembly's seat in Strasbourg.
A parliament official said Haensch had sent a letter to Wei via the Chinese authorities after the parliament decided in October to award him the prize.
"They just sent the letter back," the official told Reuters.

Former winners of the prize, instituted in 1985 as a tribute to the late Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, include South African President Nelson Mandela and Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi. ($1=.8002 Ecu)
